articles.headline: 2026 NFL playoff picture: AFC, NFC seed projections, chances
articles.description: We're looking ahead to how the 14-team playoff picture could line up -- and who will win divisions -- en route to the Super Bowl.
articles.body:
The 2026 NFL season is underway, and while it's still very early, we're already starting to track the playoff picture and the road to Super Bowl LXI. Which teams have the best chances to make the 14-team postseason field? Which have a lot of work to do to ultimately get in?

We used ESPN's Football Power Index to project the rest of the season, looking at the playoff picture for both conferences. We included updated odds for every team to make the postseason, clinch its division and even make the Super Bowl in February. Plus, we also have the FPI's projections for every game on the upcoming slate and how a win -- or a loss -- might impact each team's playoff chances, independent of other results.

Here's everything you need to know about the playoff picture right now, including which teams are trending up and down in each conference.

Jump to:

AFC picture | NFC picture

Game stakes

Trending up after Week 2: Las Vegas Raiders

Surprisingly, the Raiders are one of eight undefeated teams with new coach Klint Kubiak and veteran quarterback Kirk Cousins. And they're doing it with ease, winning each of their first two games by 12-plus points for the first time since 2002, per ESPN Research.

The Raiders began the season at No. 30 in the FPI rankings, and they're now up to No. 24 after defeating their AFC West-foe Chargers. If they can continue to get strong performances from Cousins, who had consecutive three-touchdown games for the first time in his career, Las Vegas could be a sleeper in the AFC playoff race.

Trending down after Week 2: Los Angeles Chargers

We're sticking in the AFC West, where the Chargers have had a shocking start. Our preseason FPI projections gave them a 67.7% chance at making the playoffs. They fell to 30% after losing at home to the Cardinals, and then under 10% after losing to the Raiders.

The reason for the big drop-off is simple: The Chargers' opening two games were likely their easiest of the season. DraftKings had the Chargers as at least 6.5-point favorites in both games, making them the second team in the Super Bowl era to have two such matchups to begin the year and lose them both, per ESPN Research. Now, they have the NFL's toughest schedule from Weeks 3 to 8, facing the Bills, Seahawks, Broncos, Chiefs and Rams (Week 7 bye).

Trending up after Week 2: San Francisco 49ers

While all the preseason hype in the NFC West focused on the Rams and Seahawks, it's the 49ers who have jumped to the top of the conference's playoff race. After defeating the Rams in Week 1, San Francisco's playoff odds climbed from 62.4% to 93.6%. It went up even further after an expected win over the Dolphins.

Seattle is still undefeated despite Drew Lock starting for the injured Sam Darnold, while Los Angeles bounced back in Week 2 with a dominant win over the Giants. But the 49ers have the benefit of two straight home games, starting against the Cardinals on Sunday.

articles.headline: Napoli president wants ultras out of any new stadium, warns Allegri
articles.description: With two Serie A trophies in the last four years and five other domestic cups, Napoli president Aurelio De Laurentiis is proud of what he has accomplished since rescuing the club from bankruptcy and starting in Serie C more than two decades ago.
articles.body:
With two Serie A trophies in the last four years and five other domestic cups, Napoli president Aurelio De Laurentiis is proud of what he has accomplished since rescuing the club from bankruptcy and starting in Serie C more than two decades ago.

Yet he also wants more.

De Laurentiis discussed plans for a new stadium that he hopes would be more attractive to families by keeping out hard-core "ultra" fans and sent a warning to coach Massimiliano Allegri while collecting an award recognizing his career in sports at the Foreign Press Association on Wednesday.

A film producer, De Laurentiis is one of the last Italian owners of Serie A's biggest clubs. Napoli currently play in the dilapidated Stadio Diego Armando Maradona, which is owned by the city and where sight lines are poor due to a running track.

"I have a letter of intent signed a month ago by which in eastern Naples we've found 38 hectares (94 acres) where I've planned a 70,000-seat stadium with 120 sky boxes, plus restaurants and an interactive museum," De Laurentiis said.

However, city officials have proposed renovating the Maradona stadium in time for the 2032 European Championship that Italy are co-hosting with Turkey.

De Laurentiis has had issues with the "ultras" for years and most recently made an attempt to prevent the hard-core supporters from bringing banners inside the stadium.

"Soccer should be about passion and participation. It has to be educational for kids. You can't have hooligans ... or 'ultras' that are moulded from the Mafia, 'ndrangheta and Camorra," De Laurentiis said, listing three of Italy's organized crime syndicates.

"Until our police chiefs and government ministers get the situation under control it's a major problem."

Despite the recent success, De Laurentiis has employed five different coaches since Luciano Spalletti left after leading Napoli to the Serie A title in 2023 -- their first championship since the days when Diego Maradona played for the club more than three decades earlier.

De Laurentiis was asked about Spalletti and his response could be interpreted as a warning to Allegri, Napoli's current coach, too.

Allegri is already under pressure after Napoli has won only two of six matches since he was hired to replace the departed Antonio Conte.

"Coaches need to understand that they are workers hired to direct an orchestra of footballers," said De Laurentiis, who often clashes with his coaches. "But they're still employees. Sometimes they forget that."

Despite being Serie A champion at the time, Napoli didn't qualify for the 2025 Club World Cup. And De Laurentiis doesn't sound very enthusiastic about the possibility of his club playing in the 2029 edition, either, citing too many matches.

Chelsea, who won the Club World Cup, and finalist Paris Saint-Germain played 64 and 65 matches, respectively, that season.

articles.headline: Sources: Jaxson Dart to have season-ending knee surgery
articles.description: Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart is expected to have season-ending knee surgery, sources told NFL Network.
articles.body:
New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart is expected to have season-ending knee surgery, sources told NFL Network's Ian Rapoport and Mike Garafolo.

Dart's ACL is intact, sources told Rapoport and Garafolo, and the second-year star is expected to make a full recovery.

Dart suffered damage to his MCL, PCL and meniscus, sources told ESPN's Adam Schefter.

Dart suffered the injury to his left knee during the opening possession of Monday's 28-6 loss to the Los Angeles Rams. Giants coach John Harbaugh said Tuesday that evaluations on Dart's knee were still ongoing and declined to comment further on his timeline to return.

articles.headline: Colts placing top WR Alec Pierce (heel) on IR
articles.description: The Colts are placing wide receiver Alec Pierce on injured reserve, giving him time to rehab his heel injury, coach Shane Steichen said Wednesday.
articles.body:
The Indianapolis Colts are placing wide receiver Alec Pierce on injured reserve, giving him time to rehab his heel injury, coach Shane Steichen said Wednesday.

Sources told NFL Network's Ian Rapoport earlier this week that Pierce is expected to miss several weeks after aggravating his heel injury.

By being placed on IR, Pierce is sidelined for at least the next four games. Sources told Rapoport that surgery is still on the table for Pierce but that depends on the success of his rehab efforts.

The injury is to the same heel that Pierce had surgically repaired in March. His recovery from that procedure stretched longer than expected, with him missing training camp and returning to practice only last month.

Pierce, who signed a four-year, $114 million contract in March, was expected to be a centerpiece of the Colts' offense this season. Already thin at wide receiver because of veteran backup Ashton Dulin's ankle injury, the Colts signed veteran receiver Darius Slayton this week.

Steichen said Slayton will practice Wednesday and it hasn't been ruled out that he could make his debut Sunday against the Houston Texans.

ESPN's Stephen Holder contributed to this report.

articles.headline: How San Diego Padres have become a flashpoint in MLB's labor battle
articles.description: Is San Diego why baseball needs a salary cap -- or a shining example of why it doesn't? It depends on who you ask.
articles.headlineJa: サンディエゴ・パドレスはどのようにしてMLBの労使対立における争点となったのか
articles.descriptionJa: サンディエゴは野球界にサラリーキャップが必要な理由の象徴なのか、それとも不要であることを示す好例なのか？それは誰に尋ねるかによって意見が分かれます。
articles.body:
ON THE DAY the San Diego Padres' new ownership group was introduced, Manny Machado did some quick math. When the team was sold in 2012, he noted, the purchase price was $800 million. Fourteen years later, the franchise had sold for $3.9 billion -- nearly five times the amount.

"In my business, I wish I could do that investment," said Machado, the Padres' star third baseman. "That's a great return."

At a time when Major League Baseball is attempting to upend its economic model by instituting a salary cap, the Padres have emerged as a beacon for players and union officials who believe a level playing field can exist without one.

In their minds, the Padres' late owner, Peter Seidler, provided the blueprint -- by pouring money into a small-market franchise, elevating the roster to championship contention, turning the ballpark into a destination spot and, after his death, netting a record sale price. Seidler might have absorbed losses along the way, but, in their minds, it was worth it. His peers, they believe, could and should follow.

To others, particularly those who pine for a cap-and-floor system in a new collective bargaining agreement, that rationale is incomplete.

They see the Padres as an outlier and a cautionary tale. Their sale price was inflated as a Southern California franchise in a one-sport town. Their trajectory -- spending so high that a loan was needed for liquidity, a generational talent in Juan Soto traded for the purpose of getting under the luxury tax threshold, a barren farm system and an unsustainable payroll -- is the plight of a team unable to hang with bigger spenders in an open market. Even if other franchises wanted to follow in the Padres' footsteps, they can't, league officials and rival owners argue. Their situation is unique.

MLB and the MLB Players' Association are in the midst of a contentious labor fight, and the Padres have become a convenient symbol for both sides. Of inspiration or caution. Of business acumen or reckless spending. Of the possibilities under a free-market system or the pitfalls that come with one.

"You can say it's unique, you can say it's not," said Padres infielder Jake Cronenworth, a member of the MLBPA's executive subcommittee. "But every club has the ability to do what we did -- invest in a good product on the field, invest in the community, and see what happens."

TODAY'S PADRES WOULD be unrecognizable to the 2019 iteration. That team ranked 24th in payroll and ultimately missed the playoffs for a 13th consecutive year.

"No one wanted to play here," said Machado, who joined the team that spring. "We were in the bottom tier of organizations."

The following year, in November 2020, Seidler assumed full control of the Padres, taking over as chairman after his business partner, Ron Fowler, stepped down. Over the next three years, the payroll jumped from $180 million to $225 million to more than $250 million by 2023, trailing only the New York Yankees and New York Mets.

articles.headline: Jaguars hope to get Hunter more involved in offense vs. Patriots
articles.description: Travis Hunter may see an increased role on offense for the Jaguars on Sunday against the Patriots.
articles.body:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- Travis Hunter may see an increased role on offense Sunday against the Patriots.

Hunter has played 11 offensive snaps in the Jaguars' first two games and head coach Liam Coen said Wednesday that "we're going to look at giving him some more this week."

Hunter has one catch for 8 yards and one carry for 3 yards, both of which came in the Jaguars' 34-10 season-opening victory over the Browns. He played four snaps against Cleveland and seven snaps in last Sunday's 20-13 loss to the Broncos.

The 2024 Heisman Trophy winner had 28 catches for 298 yards and a touchdown last season in the first seven games before missing the rest of the season because of a knee injury. He played 67% of the team's offensive snaps and 36% of the defensive snaps until his injury.

Hunter has played 62 defensive snaps in 2026 and has five tackles and one pass breakup.

articles.headline: Inside the basketball of 'One Tree Hill' 23 years later
articles.description: In honor of 23 years since "One Tree Hill" premiered, James Lafferty & Co. take us inside the basketball heart of the cult classic TV show.
articles.body:
WILMINGTON, N.C. -- "Are you here for the big game?" my new friend behind the car rental counter asked shortly after I touched down in Michael Jordan's hometown.

"People are saying you need to be in line by 7 a.m. if you want a chance at a decent seat," she exclaimed before I could answer.

To my surprise, my big game and her big game were one and the same: the "Hey 23" basketball game celebrating 23 years since the hit television show "One Tree Hill" first aired.

Pausing to look around Wilmington International Airport, it appeared nearly everyone arriving in town had the same purpose. Couples, families and groups of friends of all ages -- all donning black, white and royal blue, and not of the Duke Blue Devils variety.

I had counted at least seven combined "Scott" jerseys and two red Quentin Fields-inspired capes before a handmade "You can't kill Dan Scott" sign diverted my attention.

Then the same cheerful voice snapped me back into focus.

"Your car is ready. Just head to spot No. 23! See you tomorrow!"

Unclear whether my rental assignment was intentional or an omen, I grabbed the keys and stepped out into the North Carolina heat.

If a 23rd anniversary feels arbitrary, you're clearly not a "One Tree Hill" fan.

OTH's premise centered around a pair of half-brothers, Lucas (played by Chad Michael Murray) and Nathan Scott (played by James Lafferty) who starred on their high school basketball team in the fictional North Carolina small town of Tree Hill.

The beloved teen drama -- and in my entirely unbiased opinion, the most slept-on basketball show of our generation -- followed Nathan Scott, aka No. 23 and his journey from winning a state championship in high school to being recruited by Duke until his college plans were derailed by his involvement in a point-shaving scheme. Scott eventually went on to win a national title at Maryland before suffering a spinal injury the night before the NBA draft. He then mounted a comeback that started with SlamBall, then saw him play in the D-League and finally become the starting point guard for the then-Charlotte Bobcats.

In the 2000s, Nathan's evolution from a brash high school standout to a selfless NBA star left an indelible mark on a generation of fans. The Ravens never existed -- there was no Tree Hill High and no state championship banner. But for the people who watched the scripted show and the actors who portrayed the characters, the basketball was real. In the years since its historic nine-season run from 2003 to '12, it has amassed a cult following of a magnitude I couldn't quite grasp until setting foot where the show was filmed.

'Hey 23'

On Sept. 19, in front of nearly 5,000 fans at UNC Wilmington's Trask Coliseum, the show's stars, including Lafferty, Murray, Antwon Tanner, Robbie Jones, Bryan Greenberg and Stephen Colletti took the court together again.

articles.headline: Warriors' Stephen Curry says 'no drama' over unsettled contract
articles.description: Warriors star Stephen Curry said his unsettled contract extension situation will have zero impact on his play or the team's vibe entering the season.
articles.body:
With training camp set to open next week, Golden State Warriors star Stephen Curry said his unsettled contract extension situation will have zero impact on his play or the team's vibe entering the season.

"I don't want there to be no drama," Curry told ESPN on Wednesday. "No talking points. This team should be competitive and go win."

On Aug. 29, Curry became eligible for an extension of up to two years and $136.7 million off his current one-year, $62.6 million expiring deal. The Warriors immediately presented him with a menu of options, team sources said, including max money, slightly smaller pay cuts or the ability to wait and decide later, depending on what the front office could eventually generate with extra flexibility.

Curry has contemplated the choices for nearly a month and, as of this week, held off on committing to any of them. The Warriors begin practice next week in Hawaii and open the regular season on Oct. 21 in Los Angeles against the Lakers.

"It's going to happen at the right time, once I have all the information I need to make the decision that is right," Curry said. "The team's been great having that conversation back and forth. If I don't sign, it won't affect me in terms of my play or carrying that weight. But I'll make the decision when I'm ready."

Curry again made it clear that this has nothing to do with him testing free agency, calling it his "obvious goal" to remain with the Warriors for the entirety of his career.

If he opts for his max, it will significantly slash the Warriors' projected cap space next summer. Loaded with expiring contracts, they're currently projected to have more than $100 million in cap space. Curry's max -- or anything near -- would reduce it to around $45 million.

"We're in a very interesting situation," Curry said. "All the different salary cap conditions of whether I sign for a max or less or whatever it is, I want to be on a competitive team. I want to have an opportunity to have some flexibility because we haven't had that in years past, the recent past.

"... This team should have flexibility to make necessary moves if things happen. Those are always just the considerations. For me, information and patience is key. It's just a very unique situation all the way around based on where we've been the last four years, where I'm at in my career, what our team looks like this year and the absolute desperation to win. Trying to balance all that."

Curry, 38, is entering his 18th NBA season. There is clear appeal to locking into one or two more seasons at big money, but he has developed enough of a trusting relationship with general manager Mike Dunleavy and the front office to at least marinate on the choice.

Curry was limited to 43 games last season because of persistent pain and swelling in his right knee. He was in San Diego this week at a team function organized by teammate Jimmy Butler and said his body is ready for the start of training camp.
